NEW YORK (CNN) — Ariel Binns is an adorable, bright and sociable young girl who bears a striking resemblance to Sasha Obama, the younger daughter of President Obama.

Binns, a 6-year-old first-grader from Brooklyn, New York, is also a child model, and her likeness to Sasha has attracted attention in the fashion world. Harper’s Bazaar magazine selected her to appear alongside model Tyra Banks in a photo feature depicting an African-American family in the White House. In one image, Binns was shown looking out from beneath a large wooden desk, a scene that recalled the presidency of John F. Kennedy.

In fashion, a well-known and influential “brand” can be a major force in driving interest and sales — and few brands are as powerful as a popular first family. Global branding specialist David Rogers says advertisers and marketers are beginning to recognize the appeal. “Marketers are finally waking up to it — you know — black is beautiful,” Rogers said. He expects African-American models to become more visible in fashion photography because of the impact of the Obama family.

Rogers added that this kind of representation is likely to become woven into mainstream fashion images and popular culture, which he described as a very positive development.

At Wilhelmina Kids, a New York modeling agency representing children and teenagers, agents say requests have grown for models who resemble the Obama daughters. Marlene Wallach, president of Wilhelmina, which represents Binns, said the interest is part of a trend. “What little girl doesn’t want to emulate the first kids?” she said.

Branding experts say the fascination surrounding Sasha and Malia Obama is different from the attention once given to the Bush twins or Chelsea Clinton. They describe the Obama girls’ appeal as distinctive and highly marketable. One example came after the girls wore J.Crew clothing on Inauguration Day: the company’s website received so much traffic that it crashed.

Rogers said the Obamas are “the most visible, most exciting family in America,” and that their identity as a beautiful Black family has created demand for similar images. He said many Americans want to relate to the family or feel some personal connection to them.

But that attention also has drawbacks. The Obama family objected when toy company Ty Inc. introduced African-American dolls called Sweet Sasha and Marvelous Malia, although the company said the dolls were not intended to resemble the Obama daughters. Michelle Obama’s office said it was “inappropriate to use young private citizens for marketing purposes.”

New York clinical psychologist Judy Kuriansky said famous families often struggle with this kind of issue. She said she understood why Michelle Obama would want to shield her daughters, noting that many Hollywood celebrities feel the same way. Once children become part of the public image, Kuriansky said, they can be treated as if they belong to the public and can be used in many ways, which may interfere with their ability to grow up like ordinary children.

Even so, some people believe Sasha and Malia’s visibility has an important benefit: it offers a prominent and positive image of young African-American girls. When asked whether she thinks the Obama daughters could create opportunities for her own daughter, Ariel Binns’ mother, Dawn Crooks, said, “I think it will. I hope it does.”

Rogers said that, in the broader sense, the use of Obama-girl look-alikes could help push diversity in fashion and media to an entirely new stage.

## Sasha and Malia Obama and the Making of Marketable Cultural Figures

When Barack Obama entered the White House in 2009, public fascination did not stop with the new president and first lady. His daughters, Malia and Sasha Obama, were also swept into the national spotlight. Though they were children at the time, their presence carried unusual cultural power: they represented a young, modern, highly visible American family at the center of history. Almost immediately, their clothing, hairstyles, public appearances, and even their general “look” became subjects of media attention and commercial interest.

That attention helped turn the Obama daughters into marketable cultural figures, even as their parents and Michelle Obama’s office worked to protect them from being treated as celebrities or commercial brands.

### The appeal of the “first daughters”

Sasha and Malia occupied a rare public role. They were not elected officials, entertainers, or professional influencers, but they appeared on one of the world’s largest stages. Their visibility came from proximity to power and from the symbolic meaning attached to the Obama family.

As the first Black children to grow up in the White House, they were seen by many Americans as symbols of generational change. Their presence also softened the image of the presidency, presenting the Obamas as a relatable family with school schedules, homework, vacations, and ordinary parenting concerns. This combination of historic significance and everyday familiarity made them especially compelling to the public.

Because they were young, stylish, and closely associated with Michelle Obama’s widely praised fashion sense, Sasha and Malia also became figures of interest in consumer culture. What they wore could attract attention not because they endorsed anything, but because they appeared in highly photographed national moments.

### First daughter look-alikes and the market for resemblance

One sign of their cultural marketability was the emergence of “first daughter” look-alikes. In entertainment, advertising, and political satire, children resembling Sasha and Malia could be used to evoke the Obama family without directly involving the real girls. Their images became recognizable enough that resemblance itself had commercial value.

This kind of look-alike culture reflects a broader pattern in celebrity marketing. Once a public figure becomes visually familiar, advertisers, comedians, television producers, and event organizers may use imitation or suggestion to capitalize on that recognition. With Sasha and Malia, however, the practice raised sharper ethical questions because they were minors who had not chosen public careers.

A look-alike can seem harmless, especially when used playfully, but it also demonstrates how quickly children connected to political fame can be absorbed into commercial and media systems. Their identities become shorthand for an era, a family, and a political brand, even when no formal permission has been granted.

### J.Crew and the Inauguration Day fashion moment

The clearest example of the girls’ market influence came during Barack Obama’s first inauguration. Sasha and Malia wore colorful J.Crew outfits, and the brand received enormous publicity. Their coats, scarves, gloves, and coordinated looks were widely discussed in fashion coverage, helping J.Crew benefit from one of the most watched public events in the world.

The company did not need a traditional advertising campaign featuring the Obama daughters. The inauguration itself functioned as a global media platform. Photographs of the family circulated everywhere, and fashion writers quickly identified the clothing. The result was a publicity windfall.

J.Crew’s association with the Obama family also fit the brand’s image at the time: polished, accessible, preppy, and modern. Michelle Obama had already become known for mixing designer clothing with more affordable labels, and the girls’ outfits reinforced the idea that the new first family had a stylish but approachable sensibility.

For retailers, this was the power of the “first family effect.” A single public appearance could drive attention to a label, shape consumer desire, and connect a brand to broader feelings of optimism, youth, and national renewal.

### Michelle Obama’s office and concerns about commercialization

The commercial attention surrounding Sasha and Malia also created discomfort inside Michelle Obama’s office. The first lady was highly aware that her daughters were children, not public commodities. Her team often tried to draw boundaries between legitimate news coverage of the first family and attempts to profit from the girls’ images.

Concerns reportedly arose when companies or media outlets appeared to use the girls’ names, likenesses, or style for promotional purposes. The issue was not simply fashion coverage; it was the possibility that private children were being turned into marketing tools without consent.

Michelle Obama repeatedly emphasized that Sasha and Malia deserved as normal a childhood as possible. That meant limiting interviews, discouraging intrusive coverage, and resisting efforts to treat them as celebrities. Her office’s concerns reflected a broader ethical question: how much public attention is appropriate for presidential children, especially when commercial interests are involved?

### Public figures, private children

The Obama daughters’ experience illustrates the tension between visibility and privacy. As members of the first family, they inevitably appeared at major public events. Their images were part of the public record. But they were not political actors. They did not campaign in the same way adult surrogates did, and they did not seek fame.

Yet modern media culture often collapses those distinctions. The public’s affection for a political family can become consumer demand. A child’s coat becomes a fashion story. A hairstyle becomes a trend. A resemblance becomes marketable. Brands and media outlets benefit from attention that the children themselves never solicited.

This dynamic is especially powerful when the family represents a cultural milestone. The Obamas were not just another first family; they were symbols of racial progress, changing American identity, and a new generational style. Sasha and Malia were part of that symbolism, whether or not anyone intended to market them.

### The legacy of their visibility

As Sasha and Malia have grown older, they have continued to attract public interest, though they have largely maintained private lives. Their childhood in the White House remains a case study in how political celebrity, fashion culture, race, youth, and consumer marketing intersect.

They became marketable cultural figures not through personal branding, but through public fascination with the Obama family. Look-alikes, fashion coverage, and brand publicity all showed how valuable their image could become. At the same time, Michelle Obama’s office served as a reminder that marketability does not erase the need for boundaries.

The story of Sasha and Malia Obama is therefore not just about style or celebrity. It is about the ethics of attention. It asks whether admiration can become exploitation, whether public symbolism can coexist with private childhood, and how society should treat young people who become famous simply because their parents entered history.

**REPORTER:**  
For the fashion industry, the attraction is clear: imagery connected to the Obama family evokes aspiration without excess, elegance without distance, and a version of American style that feels both personal and historic.

**ANCHOR:**  
And as brands continue searching for authenticity, the visual legacy of one of America’s most recognizable families appears likely to remain part of the fashion conversation.

**ANCHOR TAG:**  
Again, any commercial use of a public figure’s image raises legal and ethical questions, including rights of publicity and permissions — especially when children are involved.

counterfactuals.output:
**Obama Daughter Look-Alikes Become a Quiet Trend in Fashion and Advertising, Raising Questions About Representation and Ethics**

In fashion campaigns, children’s catalogs and social-media advertising, a familiar visual shorthand has increasingly appeared: young Black girls styled in ways that evoke the polished, aspirational image once associated with Sasha and Malia Obama during their years in the White House.

The models are not the Obama daughters, and most ads do not name them. But industry observers say the resemblance is often hard to miss — a combination of age, styling, hair, wardrobe and “first family” cues that suggest intelligence, poise and upward mobility. The trend reflects both a broader push for diversity in advertising and a more complicated marketing instinct: borrowing the public’s affection for famous children without their participation or consent.

For brands, the appeal is obvious. The Obama family remains one of the most recognizable symbols of Black excellence in American public life. During Barack Obama’s presidency, images of his daughters offered a rare mainstream depiction of Black girlhood connected to power, education and grace rather than stereotype. Advertisers have increasingly sought to reflect that image in campaigns aimed at parents who want to see children of color represented in positive, aspirational ways.

“Representation matters, and families notice when children who look like theirs are shown as smart, stylish and central to the story,” said one marketing consultant who works with youth-focused brands. “The Obama years helped normalize an image of Black girls as part of the American ideal.”

That shift has had real benefits. Fashion and retail advertising has become more inclusive over the past decade, with more Black, brown and multiracial children appearing in back-to-school campaigns, luxury-inspired shoots and family lifestyle ads. For young consumers, seeing diverse children presented as leaders, scholars or trendsetters can help counter decades of exclusion in mainstream media.

But the practice becomes more ethically fraught when resemblance appears to be the point.

Child advocates and media ethicists warn that campaigns built around look-alikes can blur the line between representation and appropriation. Even when a celebrity child’s name or image is not used directly, advertisers may still be trading on a child’s identity, public visibility and family legacy. The concern is especially sharp when the original public figures were minors at the time they became famous.

“There is a difference between casting diverse children and deliberately evoking specific children who grew up under intense public scrutiny,” said a media ethics scholar. “If the goal is to trigger recognition, then the campaign is benefiting from an association the children did not choose.”

The Obama daughters, like other children of presidents, became public figures by circumstance rather than profession. While both are now adults, much of the public’s emotional connection to them comes from their childhood years in the White House. That makes marketing around their likeness particularly sensitive.

The issue also touches on a larger debate about children in advertising. Young models may be paid and represented by guardians or agencies, but they often cannot fully understand how their images will circulate online or how audiences may interpret them. When styling encourages comparison to famous children, the young models themselves can be placed inside a narrative they did not create.

Critics say brands should ask whether they are celebrating diversity broadly or using resemblance as a shortcut to cultural cachet. They also urge companies to avoid campaign concepts that depend on viewers making a connection to identifiable minors or former minors.

Supporters of the trend argue that the resemblance may be overstated, and that not every polished image of a Black girl in a cardigan, dress or school setting should be read through the lens of the Obama family. They say such assumptions can unfairly narrow the range of acceptable representation, as if Black children in refined or elite settings must be imitating someone famous.

That tension is at the heart of the debate. The increased visibility of Black girls in fashion and advertising is widely viewed as progress. But when brands appear to market around the aura of specific children, the progress can feel compromised.

The emerging consensus among advertising professionals is that intention and execution matter. Campaigns that feature diverse children as individuals — with distinct styling, stories and context — are less likely to raise concerns. Campaigns that rely on recognizable imitation, especially without acknowledgment or permission, risk being seen as exploitative.

As brands continue to seek authenticity in diverse representation, the lesson may be simple: celebrate the cultural impact of figures like the Obama family without turning children’s identities into marketing templates. Representation can open doors, but ethical advertising requires making sure children are not used as symbols before they are treated as people.
